local_checks.invariant: A release that fails the smoke check never stays live.
local_checks.result: smoke.py main() runs each check in a retry-until-deadline loop, accumulates `failed += problem is not None`, and returns 1 if any check failed (no early-pass path). deploy.sh runs it under `set -euo pipefail` and, on non-zero, captures `before=$(readlink current)` taken BEFORE activation (deploy.sh:95): if `before != releases/$release` it invokes rollback.sh --from-failed $release (deploy.sh:107-108) which switches `current` back to the previous history entry and restarts the services, then deploy.sh exits 1. The only non-rollback branch (deploy.sh:105) is when the failed release was already `current` before this run (same-files re-deploy) - nothing changed, so there is nothing to roll back to. The gate correctly prevents a newly switched, smoke-failing release from remaining live.

local_checks.invariant: The smoke check exercises the newly switched release, not a stale or different one.
local_checks.result: activate-release.sh switches the `current` symlink with one atomic rename and restarts mutis-api (and mutis-chain) before deploy.sh runs smoke. Caddy serves `root * /srv/mutis/app/current/dist` through the symlink and marks pages Cache-Control: no-cache (Caddyfile), so the home/manifest fetches over the public origin resolve to the just-switched dist. The manifest check binds the live artifact to the workstation build by both git_sha and the full file->hash map (smoke.py manifest()); the --api health check requires the live API to report a `version` that prefixes the deployed git_sha (smoke.py health()); the --chain check requires fresh chain_ok. Thus the checks exercise the new release's static assets and restarted API. No way found for smoke to pass against a stale release when the API is enabled.

hardening_notes: tests/e2e/smoke.py manifest() compares the live manifest's self-reported file->hash map and git_sha against the workstation build, but does not re-fetch and re-hash each served asset; served-file integrity is left to browser SRI and verify-deploy (a peer-owned release-chain unit), so a served asset whose bytes diverge from its manifest hash would not be caught by smoke alone.

With MUTIS_KEEP_CHAIN=1 the --chain smoke check reads the kept old chain worker's heartbeat via /api/v1/stats, so chain-worker code shipped in a web-only release (no migration) is not exercised by smoke until the next restart; this is the documented keep-chain path but means --chain passing does not prove the new chain code runs.

On a first-ever deploy, if smoke fails and no earlier release exists on disk, rollback.sh finds no target and exits non-zero, leaving the failing release as `current`; acceptable for initial bring-up (no prior good release) but worth an explicit guard.

Consider changing the mutis-api gate to an exact match (refuse when db.version() != SCHEMA_VERSION) and adding the same exact-match check to mutis-chain and mutis-cleanup plus a schema-version check in healthcheck.py, so a rollback onto a newer schema fails closed and turns the healthcheck red as rollback.sh already promises.

local_checks.invariant: Each request is framed exactly once on the shared Caddy-to-API connection. A body the API does not read is drained or the connection is closed.
local_checks.result: Framing breaks when the body uses Transfer-Encoding: chunked. Request.content_length is 0 when there is no Content-Length header (http_util.py:84-89). check_length refuses Transfer-Encoding before body_read is set (http_util.py:96-97). The cleanup step at api.py:347 then runs neither _drain nor a close, so the connection stays open with the chunk bytes unread. On the real API, one chunked POST /api/v1/pow and one chunked GET /api/v1/health each returned their normal response. In both cases the API then parsed the leftover chunk-size line as a second request and wrote an extra bare HTTP/0.9-style JSON 400 ('Malformed request', with no status line) on the same connection before closing it. When a different request was sent next on that connection, it was never served: it received only those stray bytes and EOF. Control: the same POST with Content-Length was followed by a correctly served next request on a connection that stayed open.

local_checks.invariant: Client identity used for limits comes only from Caddy's X-Real-IP over loopback, and a client cannot supply or duplicate it.
local_checks.result: Caddy sets X-Real-IP with header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}, replacing any copy the client sent, and removes X-Forwarded-For (Caddyfile:179-180). client_ip trusts the header only when the TCP peer is 127.0.0.1 or ::1 (ipkeys.py:56-60). The server refuses any bind except 127.0.0.1 (api.py:411-414). An unparsable value falls back to the 0.0.0.0 key and is never exempt (ipkeys.py:41-44, api.py:105-111). A client-chosen X-Real-IP could only be smuggled if attacker bytes were parsed as a request. Under the chunked desync the leftover always starts with the hex chunk-size line that Go writes, and the API answers it with a 400 and closes the connection. So no attacker-controlled request is reached on that path. Other local processes can set the header, but that depends on the ufw owner-match rules, which belong to the peer unit host-privileges.

local_checks.invariant: State-changing cross-origin requests are refused, and Caddy and the API agree on which paths are API paths.
local_checks.result: Every non-GET request with an Origin header other than cfg.origin gets 403, and 'null' is refused too (api.py:375-378). All credentials are custom headers (Authorization Bearer, X-Mutis-*), with no cookies, so there is no ambient credential for ordinary CSRF. Caddy proxies only paths that match @api /api/* after cleaning the path (Caddyfile:141,155-185). A path that starts with '//' can make Python's urlsplit read the first segment as a host (e.g. //api/api/v1/x), but it still lands on an /api/v1 route that received the same Caddy API policy. That is not a policy bypass.

local_checks.invariant: No request data reaches a response header unescaped.
local_checks.result: Response headers carry only fixed strings, integers and fixed filenames: 'sealed.bin' and 'mutis-canary-<int>.bin' in Content-Disposition (blobs.py:41-44, call sites in shares.py:515, blobs.py:106, canary.py:62), plus Retry-After from an int (http_util.py:73). No response-header injection.

local_checks.invariant: A partially read Content-Length body never leaves attacker bytes on a kept-alive connection.
local_checks.result: Only uploads.put_chunk streams a body (uploads.py:241 calls storage.write_at:53-68 through body_slices). body_read becomes True when the generator first runs, so a non-ApiError OSError partway through the body (in os.pwrite) would skip both drain and close. The leftover chunk bytes, which the attacker chooses, would then be parsed as a request from a trusted loopback peer. That needs a disk write failure after posix_fallocate has already reserved the space (storage.py:46), so it is not attacker-reachable. Recorded as hardening.

local_checks.invariant: Caddy re-frames any request body it forwards to the API with Content-Length, so the API's Content-Length-only drain logic is always reached.

local_checks.invariant: mutis-api refuses to start whenever the database schema version is not the code's SCHEMA_VERSION, including a rollback that leaves the code behind a newer, already-migrated schema (the protection rollback.sh documents).

local_checks.invariant: Some rollback target that is actually reachable (an on-disk release) has a SCHEMA_VERSION below the live database's schema version, so the strict-< gate would let older code boot on a newer schema.

local_checks.invariant: Leaf and node hashing keep separate domains (0x00 leaf, 0x01 node, separate tags for stored, exit and pad leaves), and rootFromProof follows RFC 9162 §2.1.3.2 exactly as the server's verify_inclusion does, so a non-member leaf can't reach a real root.
local_checks.result: Stored leaves are 0x00||'mutis-leaf-v1'||id16||ct_hash, exit leaves are 0x00||'mutis-exit-v1'||id16||u32be(hour), pad leaves are 0x00||'mutis-pad-v1'||rand32, and nodes are 0x01||l||r. The browser computes the leaf itself. JS and Python carry fn/sn identically, both require sn==0, index<size and safe integers, and compare in constant time (bytes.equal). Proof steps of a length other than 32 bytes can't reach a real 65-byte node preimage without a SHA-256 collision, so they can't forge membership.

local_checks.invariant: Server-generated proofs for padded checkpoint sizes verify in the browser verifier, tampered proofs don't, and make_checkpoint only produces sizes that are multiples of 64 and strictly growing.
local_checks.result: All 30 server proofs (tree sizes 64 to 448) verified in seallog.js. Wrong index, a truncated or extended path, a 31-byte step and an empty step were all rejected. The only accepted variant was 'same proof with tree_size+64' for leaves on the left side, which recomputes the identical root. That is inherent to RFC 9162 and not a forgery, because verify.js takes leafCount and root from the same on-chain checkpoint. Checkpoint sizes were [64,128,192,320,512]. The same run showed that readSealLog accepts a header with an arbitrary template_address, an arbitrary writer key and an extra AllowAll method (recorded as hardening).

local_checks.invariant: verify.ok is shown only when a leaf computed in the browser, plus the server's path, reaches a root that the component state holds for the same leafCount (and epoch). The component address, tree_size and epoch the server sends can't redirect the check to a different root.
local_checks.result: check() looks up the on-chain checkpoint by leafCount==tree_size and epoch, then verifies against onChain.root and onChain.leafCount. The leafCount values in the state strictly increase (the template asserts this), so the match is unique. A wrong component, tree_size or epoch from the server only produces verify.bad. The stored leaf uses the ct_hash this browser recorded. The exit leaf uses exit_hour from the server, which an honest server sets to the hour of the appended leaf (items.unlink). The substate comes only through the allowlisted /chain/ix proxy to Tari's public indexers. Against honest server code, a lying indexer can't turn a false claim into verify.ok: an honest server serves proofs only for checkpoints that walletd reported committed, so forging the state only flips a true result or causes verify.bad. A lying operator API is in the accepted 'server in the path' residual (README step 4 says only the direct check removes the server, and /verify doesn't offer one; see hardening).

local_checks.invariant: The component is immutable (OwnerRule::None, DenyAll default), append_root is limited to the creating signer's key badge, appends need a multiple of 64 and strictly growing leaf_count, and no template method edits or removes a checkpoint.
local_checks.result: new() sets append_root to rule!(public_key(signer)), sets the read methods (notarize, latest, get, checkpoint_count) to allow_all and the default to deny_all, with OwnerRule::None. append_root asserts is_multiple_of(64) and leaf_count > last, keeps the newest 64, increments first_index and emits a root event. notarize writes no state. get uses checked_sub and try_from, so there is no aliasing. readSealLog enforces owner_rule 'None', default DenyAll and an append_root rule of Require NonFungibleAddress on resource_01..00 with a 64-hex U256. The template address is not checked in the browser, but verify-deploy checks it against dist/seal_log.wasm out of band.

local_checks.invariant: Only the worker's own schedule submits roots (nothing in the database or jobs table can ask it to), and a checkpoint's committed state, epoch and index come from that worker's own transaction result.
local_checks.result: seal_checkpoint builds the manifest from make_checkpoint inside a transaction; the root is hex and the size an integer, so there is no injection. It is gated by checkpoint_interval_s and a seal-now flag limited to one every 600 s, and no job type reaches it. settle() runs only on rows still 'pending'. root_event takes index and epoch from the SealLog.root event of this transaction for the configured component. If that event is missing, it falls back to self.epoch(), which can only cause a false verify.bad. recover() marks unsubmitted rows as failed. Leaf idx is UNIQUE, is never reassigned, and the leaves of failed checkpoints stay in the tree prefix, so the per-size proof cache in the handler stays consistent.

local_checks.invariant: The public proof, exit and checkpoint routes disclose nothing beyond the accepted metadata, and exit receipts follow the lifecycle: an exit leaf only for a file whose ciphertext was unlinked, and no exit claim for a kept file.
local_checks.result: proof() requires an item with a ct_hash and returns leaf_hash, an index and a path only against the newest committed checkpoint. exit_receipt() returns 409 for an active link, 'none' for a file the owner keeps, 'pending' for a doomed file, and otherwise the exit leaf from items.exit_hour, which is the same floor_hour value appended in items.unlink. Restore from the Trash doesn't touch exit_hour, and exit leaves are written only in unlink after blobs.unlink. The item id, arrival and exit windows and checkpoint metadata are accepted disclosures in docs/threat-model.md (line 20). No secret, ct_hash or owner data is returned.

hardening_notes: web/app/lib/seallog.js readSealLog and web/app/ui/verify.js don't do the checks template/seal_log/README.md ('How the browser verifies a receipt', step 4) describes. template_address isn't compared with the published SealLog template, the append_root writer key isn't compared with a pinned key, and other method_access entries aren't checked (check-01 shows a state with a foreign template, a foreign writer and an extra AllowAll 'rewrite_root' method being accepted). The verify.log text still tells the user nobody can change the log. Pin the published template address and the writer key in the release (or check them against /evidence.json), and require method_access to be exactly the known read-only set plus append_root.

/verify reads the component only through the server's /api/v1/chain/ix proxy (verify.js line 218), yet verify.ok says 'the root matches the SealLog component on the Ootle'. The README advertises a 'Check directly' path for SealLog that only exists for transactions (ootle.js checkWithIndexer). Add a direct-indexer substate read for SealLog (the CSP already allows both indexers), or reword verify.ok to say the state came through our proxy.

readSealLog doesn't check that the substate in the response is the component that was requested (no substate id or address comparison), and it ignores the include_proof data the proxy requests. Today this only matters if the proxy or indexer lies.

rootFromProof accepts proof steps of any byte length. That is not exploitable given the 0x00/0x01 domain separation and SHA-256 (check-01), but rejecting any step that isn't 32 bytes is a cheap tightening.

server/mutis/handlers/uploads.py complete() reads the upload state outside the transaction and ignores the rowcount of 'UPDATE items ... AND state = uploading'. A concurrent abort or expiry of the same upload still appends a stored leaf for a file that was never stored (with no matching exit leaf) and adds to the uploader's own used_bytes. Only the uploader's own record and quota are affected; checking rowcount == 1 before the append and the quota update would fix it.

verify.js check() dereferences res.proof.next_checkpoint_eta when leaf_index is null. For an exit receipt of 'none' (a link ended on a kept file), proof is null, so it throws, and the catch replaces the stored-receipt line with an error banner. This is a functional bug, not a security issue.

tools/verify-deploy.py seallog_check checks only the template bytes of the live log, not its owner_rule or append_root rule. A log created with an owner from the same template would pass that tool (though not the browser's readSealLog).

local_checks.invariant: A malformed or hostile upstream UTXO-stream answer is rejected as a bounded upstream error, not turned into an uncaught exception or an attacker-scaled allocation that stalls the mirror.
local_checks.result: parse_stream (indexer.py:156-174) feeds untrusted stream fields straight into int(sos['shard']), int(u['tag']) and bytes(u['public_nonce']).hex() with no type or size validation. A string public_nonce raises TypeError; an integer public_nonce makes bytes(N) allocate N attacker-chosen zero-bytes (measured: 50,000,000 bytes from an 8-digit JSON number, ~6.25M x amplification; a 10-digit number -> ~10 GB -> MemoryError). mirror() (chain_worker.py:216-233) catches only IndexerError, so this ValueError/TypeError/MemoryError aborts the entire mirror cycle (including the healthy second upstream) and the per-indexer cursor db.tx (chain_worker.py:246-255) is never reached, so the poisoned stream is re-fetched and re-fails on every 3 s tick -- permanent head-of-line blocking of the UTXO mirror that feeds all deliveries and payment detection.

local_checks.invariant: Per-output fields from the indexer are shape-validated before they reach the mirror or a credit decision.
local_checks.result: parse_fetched (indexer.py:177-192) requires commitment and nonce to be 64-char lowercase hex, enc even-length lowercase hex, and tag an int in [0, 2^32); reveals/one_time_key/substate_output (indexer.py:195-231) constrain promise to a non-negative int, auth to a short alpha name, and auth_key/one-time keys to 64-hex via _HEX32. The stream path (parse_stream) is the unvalidated one, reported as the candidate above.

local_checks.invariant: Blast radius and recovery claims match deployment-visible source.
local_checks.result: Default indexers are indexer-b then indexer-a (config.py:66), so a bad indexer-b blocks both. The healthcheck flags mirror_lagging RED (healthcheck.py:93-94) but nothing recovers automatically. chain_utxos feeds the browser scan (handlers/chain.py:54) and payment scans (chain_worker.py:288). mutis-chain has MemoryMax=1G and Restart=always (mutis-chain.service:17,54), so a large integer nonce could OOM-kill the worker. local_checks.invariant: Every egress_ok charge must read the item's egress counter inside the same BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction that writes it, so concurrent charges serialize (check-then-act cannot race), keeping bytes served per item per UTC day within EGRESS_PER_ITEM_DAY.

Under PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL (db.py:21) readers see the last committed snapshot, so a wave of concurrent requests all read the same egress_bytes before any write commits and each writes used+size from the same stale `used` -> the per-item daily counter advances by one `size` while N downloads of `size` bytes are authorized. This is the exact race db.tx (db.py:33 'BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the lock up front, so check-then-act code can't race') is meant to prevent; stored_bytes defeats it by reading outside the tx. me.open_item (me.py:212-223) and shares _open_in_tx (shares.py:405-437) read the item INSIDE the tx, so they are not affected.

local_checks.invariant: Two concurrent charges modelled on stored_bytes' stale-read sequence must not authorize more bytes than they record against the per-item daily egress counter.

hardening_notes: web/app/lib/dom.js:24 UNSAFE_URL /^\s*(javascript|vbscript|data):/i misses schemes that browsers normalize: a leading C0 control (\x01javascript:) or a tab/newline inside the scheme (java\tscript:). No attacker-controlled href reaches h() today, and app_csp (script-src 'self', Trusted Types) blocks javascript: navigation. Still, parse with new URL(value, location.href) and allowlist the protocols http:, https: and blob: instead of the regex.

web/site/js/judges.js:31-41 saves any well-formed judge pass from a /judges#pass=… link into localStorage without asking. A crafted link can plant someone else's pass, so the victim's anonymous requests carry that pass. Consider asking the visitor to confirm before saving a pass from a link.

web/app/lib/store.js:44-57 keeps up to 20 anonymous drops' manage tokens (which can delete those items) in localStorage. They are not tied to a drive and survive Lock my drive. This is documented as a per-device convenience. A 'forget this browser' action could offer to clear mutis.recent as well.
